slides.title: Brand
slides.body: Welcome!
slides.notes: The opening mark. Content rule 21 keeps "Welcome to today's session" for the next frame, so this one says something else.
slides.label: Brand

slides.title: Welcome
slides.notes: The session name, in minimal mode: the kicker and the title, nothing else.
slides.label: Welcome

slides.title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
slides.body: Recap
slides.notes: The TR's recap block: the five agenda items of the previous session, in its words. It uses the takeaways layout, not `RecapSlide`: five items with their sub lines run under the control cluster in `RecapSlide`'s two columns, and `align-check.mjs` reported it. The slide names the topic and never the session number (content rule 2b). Ask which one the room is least sure of before moving on.
slides.label: Recap

slides.title: What We Will Cover
slides.notes: The TR's agenda, all five items, split at the colon it writes. These exact strings come back on the Key Takeaways frame (content rule 20).
slides.label: Agenda

slides.title: Section: Cloud Deployment Models
slides.notes: TR section 1. The subtitle is the agenda's own sub for this section.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: Four Ways To Deploy
slides.body:
Deployment Models Map
Every workload needs infrastructure somewhere, and no single arrangement of ownership, location and sharing suits every organisation's control and compliance needs.
Infrastructure Choice
Fully shared
Fully dedicated
Public cloud
provider-owned, shared across tenants
Community cloud
shared by organisations with common needs
Hybrid cloud
private and public linked together
Private cloud
dedicated, either on-premise or hosted
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Four boxes labelled Public, Private, Hybrid, Community arranged around a central 'Infrastructure Choice' node, arrows showing a spectrum from fully shared to fully dedicated." The four TR bullets are the four boxes' own lines, so the strings appear once. They are ordered along the spectrum rather than in the TR's list order, because the spectrum is the argument. TR speaker notes: "Frame deployment choice as a spectrum from fully shared to fully dedicated infrastructure. A common exam question gives a scenario and asks which model fits it best."
slides.label: Deployment models map

slides.title: Shared Multi-Tenant Infrastructure
slides.body:
Public Cloud
A provider such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) builds and operates the data centres, then rents capacity to any customer over the internet on shared hardware.
Infrastructure owned and run entirely by the provider
Many tenants share hardware, isolated logically from each other
Capacity scales rapidly across resources pooled across customers
Best fit: variable workloads, fast launch, low compliance limits
Cloud Service Provider
Enterprise P
Enterprise Q
User R
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN. It is embedded in the document between the lead and the bullets and the text read drops it. Provider in the middle, Enterprise P and Q on either side, User R below, every arrow pointing outward from the provider. TR visual guidance: "One large building labelled 'Provider Data Centre' with multiple small logos (different companies) drawing from it over an internet cloud icon." TR speaker notes: "Note that AWS, Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) are the leading public cloud providers offering this shared model. Interviewers often test whether a given scenario needs public or private cloud based on tenancy and control."
slides.label: Public cloud

slides.title: Analogy: a shared cab
slides.body:
Public Cloud
A shared cab
Public cloud
Many riders share one vehicle
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A shared cab is owned by the cab company; many riders book seats and pay only for the ride taken, never owning the vehicle — just as public cloud tenants share provider-owned servers and pay only for the capacity used." Say it; the frame plays it. The riders light in turn on the left and the tenants light in the same order on the right.
slides.label: Analogy: a shared cab

slides.title: On-Premise Vs Hosted
slides.body:
Private Cloud
Private cloud dedicates infrastructure to one organisation only, chosen when compliance, data residency or latency needs rule out shared public hardware.
On-Premise Private Cloud
Enterprise P
Private cloud
Externally Hosted Private Cloud
Cloud Service Provider
Dedicated for Enterprise P
Other servers
Enterprise P
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN, and it is the TR's Visual Guidance as well: "Split diagram: left shows a building icon inside an organisation's fence (on-premise); right shows the same dedicated building inside a provider's larger data centre fence (hosted)." The dashed fence is the thing to point at: on the left it is the organisation's own wall, on the right it is the provider's, and the dedicated server inside it is the only lit one.
slides.label: Private cloud

slides.title: On-Premise Vs Hosted
slides.body:
Private Cloud
Aspect
On-Premise Private
Hosted Private
Location
Organisation's own data centre
Provider's data centre, dedicated section
Owned by
The organisation itself
Provider, leased to one customer
Example
In-house VMware or OpenStack cluster
VMware Cloud on AWS
Control
Full physical and logical control
Full logical control, no physical access
slides.notes: Four rows, values exactly as the TR sets them. TR speaker notes: "Contrast on-premise physical custody against hosted convenience using the table on screen. A frequent interview question asks which private cloud variant suits a bank that must keep servers within its own walls."
slides.label: Private cloud table

slides.title: Analogy: a house or a bungalow
slides.body:
Private Cloud
Build a house or rent a bungalow
On-premise or hosted private cloud
Both are yours alone
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Building a house on owned land gives full control forever; renting a private bungalow built by a developer gives the same exclusivity without construction effort — just as on-premise private cloud means owned infrastructure, while hosted private cloud means dedicated but provider-managed infrastructure." Left half of each scene is the owned one, right half the provided one.
slides.label: Analogy: a house or a bungalow

slides.title: Cloud Bursting Explained
slides.body:
Hybrid Cloud
Hybrid cloud links private and public infrastructure so workloads move between them, avoiding the need to size on-premise capacity for rare demand peaks.
Private cloud
Public cloud
Enterprise P
Enterprise Q
Cloud Service Provider
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN: a private cloud plus a public cloud, with the plus sign carrying the claim. It is embedded between the lead and the bullets and the text read drops it. The next frame says what moves across the link, and when.
slides.label: Hybrid cloud

slides.title: Cloud Bursting Explained
slides.body:
Hybrid Cloud
Sudden overload bursts into public cloud capacity temporarily
Cloud bursting: automatic overflow triggered by demand thresholds
Example: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure into on-premise sites
Private Infrastructure
Public Cloud
burst
threshold
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Two linked boxes, 'Private Infrastructure' and 'Public Cloud', with a dashed arrow labelled 'burst' flowing from private to public only when a load gauge crosses a threshold line." The gauge fills, and only after it passes the line does the arrow appear and the public box light. Watch one full loop before talking. TR speaker notes: "Stress that bursting is temporary and automatic, not a permanent migration of workloads. A common interview question asks how hybrid architecture avoids over-provisioning private capacity for rare peaks."
slides.label: Cloud bursting

slides.title: Analogy: a banquet hall
slides.body:
Hybrid Cloud
A banquet hall for the rush
Cloud bursting
Extra capacity only while the rush lasts
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A restaurant kitchen handles daily orders alone, but during a wedding rush it hires a banquet hall's ovens for the overflow and releases them once the rush ends — just as cloud bursting shifts excess load to public cloud only during demand spikes." The right-hand ovens and the right-hand rack light and fade on the same beat as the gauge swings.
slides.label: Analogy: a banquet hall

slides.title: Shared Among Peers
slides.body:
Community Cloud
Community cloud is infrastructure shared by several organisations with common regulatory, security or mission needs, rather than opened to the general public.
Governance and compliance rules set jointly by member organisations
Cost split among fewer tenants than public, more than solo private
Example: AWS GovCloud (US), reserved for government agencies and partners
Typical users: government bodies, healthcare consortiums, research collaborations
Shared infrastructure
Community cloud
Government
Healthcare
Research
General public: not admitted
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN (its heading reads "Commmunity Users", a typo in the source), and the TR's Visual Guidance fits it: one shared block, matching organisation icons for government, healthcare and research, ringed off from the general public. TR speaker notes: "Position community cloud as narrower than public but broader than private, sized to one sector's shared compliance need. An interviewer may ask why a government agency would pick AWS GovCloud over standard public cloud."
slides.label: Community cloud

slides.title: Section: Multi-Cloud
slides.notes: TR section 2.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: Multiple Providers Together
slides.body:
Multi-Cloud Defined
Multi-cloud means running workloads across two or more independent public providers at once, unlike hybrid cloud, which mixes public with private infrastructure.
Your company
aws
AWS handles general-purpose compute and storage workloads
azure
Azure serves Microsoft-integrated enterprise applications
gcp
GCP powers data analytics and AI/ML pipelines
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Diagram: one company icon with three arrows branching to AWS, Azure and GCP logos, each labelled with a workload type." The three workload lines ARE the TR's three bullets, beside the marks they belong to, so each string appears once. TR speaker notes: "Stress that multi-cloud is a deliberate split among public providers, not a synonym for hybrid cloud. A common interview question asks to differentiate multi-cloud from hybrid cloud with an example."
slides.label: Multi-cloud defined

slides.title: Multiple Providers Together
slides.body:
Multi-Cloud Defined
Multi-Cloud Strategy
Hybrid Cloud Strategy
Private Cloud
Public Cloud
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN AND CORRECTED. The source image captions the Azure mark "Azure" and then the Google Cloud mark "Azure" as well; here every mark carries its own name, which is the point of the picture. Left: several public providers together. Right: one private cloud linked to a public one.
slides.label: Multi-cloud against hybrid

slides.title: Analogy: two banks
slides.body:
Multi-Cloud Defined
Two banks for your savings
Multi-cloud
One fails, the work carries on
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Spreading savings across two different banks guards against one bank freezing withdrawals or raising fees — just as multi-cloud spreads workloads across providers so one outage or price hike does not stop operations." One side goes dark with a padlock on it while the other keeps working, on both scenes at once.
slides.label: Analogy: two banks

slides.title: Resilience Negotiation Regulation
slides.body:
Multi-Cloud Motivations
Three business pressures push organizations toward multiple providers even though it adds complexity.
Resilience
a second provider keeps services running during an outage
Negotiation leverage
comparing quotes across vendors avoids one-sided pricing
Regulation
in-country hosting or concentration-risk rules may require a compliant region or a second provider
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Three labelled icons (shield, handshake, gavel) mapped to resilience, negotiation and regulation respectively." The three bullets are the cards' own lines, split at the colon the TR writes. TR speaker notes: "Walk through each motivation with a one-line business scenario before naming it. Interviewers frequently ask why a company would choose multi-cloud over a single vendor — resilience, leverage and compliance form the three-part answer."
slides.label: Multi-cloud motivations

slides.title: Managing Multiple Platforms
slides.body:
Operational Overhead Cost
Multi-cloud earns its resilience and leverage at a real operational price: every added provider multiplies what must be learned, managed and paid for.
Separate consoles, APIs and billing dashboards per provider
Distinct certifications and skill sets needed for each platform's staff
Cross-cloud data transfer (egress) charges between providers
Duplicate monitoring, security and IAM (identity and access management) policies to maintain
aws
azure
gcp
Skills
Tooling
Billing
Security
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Table-style graphic: rows for Skills, Tooling, Billing, Security, each row showing duplicated icons across AWS/Azure/GCP columns." The same icon three times in a row IS the claim: the work is repeated per provider. The TR writes "IAM" without saying what it stands for, so it is expanded here (content rule 24). TR speaker notes: "Frame overhead as the price paid for multi-cloud's benefits, not a separate flaw. A typical exam question asks to list the operational costs of running a multi-cloud environment."
slides.label: Operational overhead

slides.title: Quiz time
slides.notes: The first quiz frame, immediately after the second topic (the position the first deck used). It tests the four deployment models and what multi-cloud is, which every later section assumes. It carries no question and no subtitle (content rules 18 and 28): the questions are asked from the quiz tool.
slides.label: Quiz time

slides.notes: TR section 3.

slides.title: Stack Ownership Map
slides.body:

The three service models share one technology stack; each shifts the line dividing provider-managed layers from customer-managed layers.
IaaS

Operating system

Customer manages
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Horizontal stack bar split into four layers, shaded by owner colour for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS side by side." The TR's own table has five layers, so the stack has five. Blue is the provider and amber is the customer, here and on every frame of this section. Only the ownership line moves; the stack does not. TR speaker notes: "Point out that only the ownership line moves, not the stack itself. Interviewers often test whether a named service can be placed on the correct layer."

slides.title: Raw Infrastructure Rental
slides.body:
IaaS Explained
Infrastructure as a Service rents compute, storage and network as raw building blocks, leaving the operating system and everything above it to the customer.
Abstracts physical hardware, racking and data-centre wiring
Customer installs OS, runtime, middleware and application
Representative services: AWS (Amazon Web Services) EC2, EBS, VPC
Azure Virtual Machines, GCP Compute Engine offer same layer
IaaS
Compute
provider
Storage
provider
Network
provider
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN: a cloud labelled IaaS with three connectors down to storage, compute and network. It is embedded after the bullets and the text read drops it. All three tiles are provider-managed blue, because the rented thing is only the raw blocks. TR speaker notes: "IaaS gives maximum control at the cost of managing everything above hardware. Interviewers often ask to map EC2 or a virtual machine to this layer."
slides.label: IaaS

slides.title: Analogy: a kitchen only
slides.body:
IaaS Explained
Kitchen space only
IaaS
You bring everything above the oven
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Domino's kitchen space and oven are used, but the dough, sauce and toppings are supplied separately and the pizza is cooked from scratch — just as the IaaS provider manages only the physical infrastructure while the customer manages the operating system, runtime and application." Amber layers slide in: three of the four are the customer's. The same four layers carry across all three pizza frames.
slides.label: Analogy: a kitchen only

slides.title: Ready-Made Platform
slides.body:
PaaS Explained
Platform as a Service adds a managed operating system and runtime atop infrastructure, so the customer only builds, deploys and runs application code.
Abstracts OS patching, runtime setup and server scaling
Less control over OS-level tuning than IaaS allows
Representative services: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AWS App Runner
Azure App Service, GCP App Engine offer same layer
PaaS
Operating system
provider
Runtime
provider
Your application
customer
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN: a cloud labelled PaaS above the managed pieces and the one thing the customer brings. The provider tiles are blue and the application is amber. TR speaker notes: "PaaS trades some flexibility for less operational work than IaaS. Interviewers often ask why Elastic Beanstalk beats raw EC2."
slides.label: PaaS

slides.title: Analogy: a kitchen with dough ready
slides.body:
PaaS Explained
Kitchen and dough ready
PaaS
You bring only the toppings
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Domino's kitchen, oven and ready dough are already set up, so only assembling and baking the pizza on that setup remains — just as the PaaS provider manages infrastructure, operating system and runtime while the customer manages only the application." One amber layer this time, against three on the IaaS frame.
slides.label: Analogy: a kitchen with dough ready

slides.title: Complete Application Delivered
slides.body:
SaaS Explained
Software as a Service delivers a finished application; the provider manages every layer beneath it, leaving the customer only account setup and data.
Abstracts the entire stack below the application
Provider pushes feature updates automatically, no customer action
Representative services: Gmail/Google Workspace, Salesforce, Microsoft 365
Customer effort and control both fall sharply toward SaaS
SaaS
Finished application
provider
Automatic updates
provider
Your data
customer
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN: a cloud labelled SaaS delivering a finished application to several devices. The only amber tile is the customer's own data. TR speaker notes: "SaaS trades all control for zero operational burden, completing the IaaS-PaaS-SaaS spectrum. Interviewers often ask to classify Gmail or a CRM tool by service model."
slides.label: SaaS

slides.title: Analogy: a ready-made pizza
slides.body:
SaaS Explained
A ready-made pizza
SaaS
You bring nothing but an order
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A ready-made pizza is ordered directly from Domino's with no kitchen work at all — just as SaaS provider manages the entire stack while the customer only uses the finished application." No amber layer is left: the finished thing is handed over.
slides.label: Analogy: a ready-made pizza

slides.title: Section: Beyond the Big Three
slides.notes: TR section 4.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: New Service Models
slides.body:
Beyond The Big Three
Cloud service models did not stop at IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Two further models push abstraction higher, changing what the provider manages and what the developer retains.
Function as a Service (FaaS): runs code per trigger, no visible server
Serverless: broader term covering FaaS plus managed databases and queues
AI/ML-as-a-Service: consumes pre-built AI and ML models via API
Both shift most infrastructure responsibility onto the cloud provider
IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
FaaS / Serverless
AI/ML-as-a-Service
Rising abstraction
User responsibility shrinks
Provider
User
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Spectrum diagram: IaaS -> PaaS -> SaaS -> FaaS/Serverless -> AI/ML-as-a-Service, arrow showing rising abstraction and shrinking user responsibility." The bar lengths are a SCHEMATIC of the direction, stepped evenly: they are not measurements, and the table two sections on is where the real split is stated per model. TR speaker notes: "Position FaaS and AI/ML-as-a-Service as the next step beyond the three classic models, removing the server concept entirely. Interviewers often ask where FaaS sits relative to PaaS on the abstraction ladder."
slides.label: Beyond IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

slides.title: Pay Per Execution
slides.body:
FaaS And Serverless
Function as a Service (FaaS) runs a single function only when triggered, removing any need to provision or manage a server.
Triggers: HTTP request, scheduled timer, queue message, file upload
Scales automatically from zero to many parallel invocations
Billed per invocation and execution time, not idle time
Runs on AWS Lambda; cold start delay if idle first
slides.notes: The TR's lead and four bullets, as written. The timeline that draws them is the next frame, because beside four bullets it would have to be squeezed under the width where five stops stay readable. TR speaker notes: "Emphasise that FaaS removes even the persistent runtime instance PaaS still manages. Interview question: differentiate FaaS from PaaS by billing granularity."
slides.label: FaaS and serverless

AWS Lambda
billed only while it runs

slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Timeline: idle -> trigger event -> function instantiated -> executes -> torn down, labelled with AWS Lambda." The bracket under the middle three is the third bullet drawn: billing counts the running part and not the idle ends.
slides.label: A function's life

slides.title: Analogy: a cab for one trip
slides.body:
FaaS And Serverless
A cab for one trip
Function as a Service
Pay only while it runs
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Booking a cab only when travel is needed and paying just for that ride, instead of owning an idle car, mirrors FaaS: code runs only on a trigger and billing counts only execution time." The idle owned car and the idle rack are the two dimmed things.
slides.label: Analogy: a cab for one trip

slides.title: Pre-Built Intelligence APIs
slides.body:
AI ML As Service
AI/ML-as-a-Service (Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning as a Service) exposes pre-trained vision, language and forecasting models through a plain API call.
Representative services: Amazon Rekognition, Comprehend (pre-built APIs)
Provider manages model training, GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) and hosting
User manages input data and API integration only
Used in vision, chatbots, fraud and forecasting
slides.notes: The TR's lead and four bullets, as written, with the flow that draws them on the next frame. TR speaker notes: "Distinguish SageMaker, a full ML platform, from Rekognition and Comprehend, narrow pre-built APIs. Interviewers often ask when to call a managed AI service instead of training a custom model."
slides.label: AI/ML-as-a-Service

One consultation, no hospital
AI/ML-as-a-Service

slides.label: Analogy: a specialist doctor

slides.title: Section: Cloud Economics & Providers

slides.title: Costs And Providers
slides.body:
Cloud Economics Map
Cloud adoption decisions turn on how spending is structured and who supplies the infrastructure.
CapEx vs OpEx
how spend is classified
TCO
true multi-year cost of a choice
Pricing models
on-demand, committed use, spot
Providers
global hyperscalers and Indian regional players
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Four-quadrant map, one label per quadrant: CapEx/OpEx, TCO, Pricing Models, Providers." The four bullets are the four quadrants, split at the colon the TR writes, so each string appears once. TR speaker notes: "Set up the four building blocks of cloud economics before going deep into each. Exam and interview questions often ask to classify a cost or pick the right pricing model for a scenario."
slides.label: Cloud economics map

slides.title: Balance Sheet Impact
slides.body:
CapEx vs OpEx
Cloud does not just change how much is paid; it changes which financial statement absorbs the cost, reshaping approvals and tax treatment.
CapEx: capitalised, depreciated over asset life, sits on balance sheet
OpEx: expensed immediately, hits the income statement same period
Balance sheet
CapEx
depreciated over time
Income statement
OpEx
the same each month
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Split panel: balance sheet with a depreciation curve versus income statement with a flat recurring expense line." The left bars step down because a capitalised asset is written off over its life; the right bars are level because a monthly expense is the same every month. Both are drawn from arrays, so the shapes are data. The TR has six bullets; this frame carries the two that define the terms and the next carries the four that follow from them.
slides.label: CapEx vs OpEx

slides.title: Balance Sheet Impact
slides.body:
CapEx vs OpEx
CapEx typically needs board-level capital approval
OpEx approval sits within departmental budgets
Depreciation deductions (CapEx) shift tax timing versus OpEx's immediate deduction
AWS Cost and Usage Report classifies spend for finance systems
slides.notes: The TR's last four bullets, as written. TR speaker notes: "Stress that AWS invoices are OpEx by default, which is why finance teams favour the flexibility. Interviewers often ask why cloud shifted budgeting power from capital committees to individual teams."
slides.label: CapEx vs OpEx, continued

slides.title: Analogy: a house on a loan, or rent
slides.body:
CapEx vs OpEx
A house on a loan, or rent
CapEx and OpEx
One is an asset, one is a monthly cost
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Buying a house needs a large loan and years of EMIs recorded as an asset, while renting is a monthly expense with nothing recorded — just as CapEx locks value on the balance sheet while OpEx flows straight through the income statement." On the left a recorded asset shrinks as it is written off; on the right a small payment leaves every beat.
slides.label: Analogy: a house on a loan, or rent

slides.title: Beyond The Price Tag
slides.body:
Total Cost Ownership
Total cost of ownership (TCO) totals every direct and indirect cost of running a workload across its life, not only the sticker price.
Direct costs: compute, storage, licensing, network transfer
Indirect costs: staffing, training, downtime, migration effort
On-premise adds power, cooling, floor space, hardware refresh
AWS Pricing Calculator estimates cloud cost
Migration Evaluator builds the on-premise vs cloud business case
Sticker price
Staffing
Power
Downtime
True cost of ownership
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Layered bar: sticker price at the base, staffing/power/downtime stacked above it to show true TCO." The fourth bullet's trailing full stop is dropped. TR speaker notes: "Emphasise that TCO, not sticker price, is the number that should justify a migration. TCO comparisons are a favourite whiteboard question when interviewers test cloud cost reasoning."
slides.label: Total cost of ownership

slides.title: Analogy: a smartphone
slides.body:
Total Cost Ownership
A phone's price tag
Server TCO
The price tag is only the start
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A smartphone's price tag ignores the data plan, repairs and accessories bought over its life — just as a server's purchase price ignores the staffing, power and downtime that TCO adds back in." The three blocks stack up one after another beside the price tag on both sides.
slides.label: Analogy: a smartphone

slides.title: On-Demand To Spot
slides.body:
Three Pricing Models
Providers meter usage but let buyers trade commitment for discount; three payment patterns cover most cloud spend.
On-demand: metered pay-as-used rate, zero commitment
Committed use: one to three-year term for lower fixed rate
Spot: spare capacity at a steep discount; can be reclaimed at short notice
Trade-off across all three: flexibility versus price
On-Demand
Committed Use
Spot
Price falls
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Three tickets side by side, labelled On-Demand, Committed Use, Spot, with a price arrow decreasing left to right." The bar on each ticket is a SCHEMATIC of the order of price, not a quoted figure; the real discounts are on the comparison frame two slides on. TR speaker notes: "Frame on-demand as the metered billing model already familiar from pay-per-use pricing. Interviewers ask when to pick spot versus reserved capacity for a given workload."
slides.label: Three pricing models

slides.title: Analogy: three train tickets
slides.body:
Three Pricing Models
Three kinds of train ticket
On-demand, committed, spot
Less flexibility, lower price
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A general train ticket costs full fare and needs no planning, a season pass costs less for a fixed daily route, and a standby ticket is cheapest but the seat can be given away — just as on-demand, committed use and spot trade flexibility for price." The right-hand ticket and the right-hand rack both flicker: that is the one that can be given away.
slides.label: Analogy: three train tickets

slides.title: Regional Alternatives
slides.body:
Indian Cloud Providers
Alongside global hyperscalers, Indian providers compete on data residency, latency for local users, and rupee-denominated billing.
CtrlS, Yotta, E2E Networks: private data-centre players
Government's GI Cloud (MeghRaj) hosts public-sector workloads
BFSI (banking, financial services and insurance) and government workloads often mandate in-country storage
Regional providers can undercut hyperscaler pricing for local traffic
Inside India
CtrlS
Yotta
E2E Networks
GI Cloud (MeghRaj)
Global hyperscalers
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Map of India with data-centre pins beside the hyperscaler logos for scale comparison." It is NOT drawn as a map. A map has to draw India's border, a legally contested line, and an outline traced by hand at this size carries no real geography either way; content rule 8 prefers a typographic frame to a misleading picture. Every other element is here: one pin per provider inside an in-country zone, the three hyperscaler marks beside it. TR speaker notes: "Note that data-residency and sector regulation, not just price, drive some workloads to Indian providers. This regulatory angle is a common follow-up question after any provider-comparison discussion." The TR writes "BFSI" without expanding it; it is expanded here (content rule 24).
slides.label: Indian cloud providers
